title: Inference economics sprint — Aurum Financial constraints review
summary: Kickoff sprint to map Aurum's inference cost constraints, latency targets, and hosting preferences. Focus on per-token unit economics, batching and KV/prefix cache opportunities, and tradeoffs between Hosted, Dedicated, and Private (VPC/on-prem). Next steps: tailored pricing sheet, benchmark plan, security doc bundle.
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
action_items: Sofia Chen: prepare tailored pricing spreadsheet showing per-token breakouts for hosted and dedicated; include 6/12 month commit options — due 2025-07-06
Marcus Li: propose benchmark test plan and sample prompt set; include latency SLO targets and quantized model variants — due 2025-07-08
Tanya Gomez: share typical request size distribution and 95th perc latency constraint anonymized from prod — due 2025-07-04
next_steps: Redwood to send pricing spreadsheet and security pack (SOC2 + network diagrams)
Schedule a 2-hour benchmark window for week of 2025-07-14 (Marcus to lead)
Customer to share spike-week traffic profile and top 50 prompts
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-07-02 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Li (Redwood SE), Carla Diaz (CFO - Aurum), Raj Patel (Eng Lead - Aurum), Tanya Gomez (ML Infra - Aurum)

Auto-summary (may be imperfect): map budgets to hosting; primary anchor is per-token unit economics, but customer also cares about deterministic latency for trading-use cases.

00:00 - 00:34 Sofia Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, really quick intro — i'm sofia from Redwood, and Marcus is our systems eng, we run inference perf and pilots. Carla, Raj, Tanya, thanks for making time. do you want quick intros?
00:35 - 01:10 Carla Diaz: yeah sure, i'm carla, cfo at aurum, overseeing cost and vendor decisions, we're evaluating how to run LLMs for customer support and internal insights. timeline — hoping to decide Q3.
01:11 - 01:44 Raj Patel: hi all, raj here. we own infra and will own the pilot. main concerns: tail latency under burst, and control over data custody.
01:45 - 02:12 Tanya Gomez: tanya, ml infra. curious about caching, kv and how batching would affect our SLA. we have a lot of short queries — average token length maybe 18, but a smaller subset are long dialogues.
02:13 - 02:55 Marcus Li: great, quick note — we usually look at request distribution (tokens per request), percent of long sessions, and can recommend batching/kv configs; also can show dedicated pools if you want capacity isolation.

03:00 - 04:05 Sofia Chen: objective for today: map your budget envelope and latency targets to hosting options. specifically per-token target price and whether you'd accept dedicated commit vs hosted on pay-as-you-go. Carla, can you share the budget constraints?
04:06 - 05:02 Carla Diaz: high level — we have an internal cap of $120k per month for inference across two products to start. ideally per-customer feature cost should be under $0.004 per conversation for the majority of cases. that's a crude target.
05:03 - 05:45 Raj Patel: to add, our P95 latency needs to be under 400ms for short prompts — those are critical for live trading desk summaries (not the first phase but a future requirement).
05:46 - 06:28 Marcus Li: okay that's helpful. small prompts + tight P95 usually push us toward dedicated or private with warm caches unless you accept a slightly higher per-token cost for hosted with guaranteed low-latency tiers.

06:30 - 07:30 Tanya Gomez: quick q — you mentioned KV cache and prefix cache. how often do we see hit rates that matter; if most of our queries are short and repetitive, does that drop token consumption significantly?
07:31 - 08:12 Marcus Li: yes. typical prefix/KV caching can reduce up to 30-60% token compute for high-repeat workloads. but it depends on prompt similarity; for unique customer queries it's limited. we can instrument and estimate based on a sample trace.
08:13 - 09:00 Raj Patel: we can give you a 48-hour sample trace of anonymized requests, is that enough?
09:01 - 09:42 Marcus Li: that's perfect. from that we can estimate effective tokens saved, batching potential, and recommend instance types / quantization profiles.

09:45 - 11:00 Carla Diaz: on pricing — what does Redwood charge per token and how does that change for dedicated commitments? we need a model to plug into our financials.
11:01 - 12:05 Sofia Chen: short answer — hosted per-token rates vary by model and perf tier. with dedicated reserved capacity we do commit pricing which reduces unit cost and gives predictable throughput. we'll send a sheet, but high level: hosted might be 15-30% higher per token versus deeply committed dedicated pools.
12:06 - 12:50 Carla Diaz: okay can you give an example — we run 10M requests / mo with avg 25 tokens, how does that translate?
12:51 - 13:40 Marcus Li: rough math: 10M * 25 = 250M tokens. multiply by model cost; with hosted at say $0.000012/token (example) that's $3k — wait, that seems off — transcription, hold on — i mean $3k is too low for our models. maybe better to show a detailed calc in the sheet. (crosstalk)
13:41 - 14:20 Sofia Chen: yeah we'll avoid giving a one-off number live, we'll produce a scenario table: hosted, small commit, large commit, and on-prem license if relevant.

14:22 - 15:20 Raj Patel: security is non-negotiable for us. SOC2 is standard — but we need details on key management (bring-your-own-key), audit logs, and network segmentation for Private. can Redwood run in our VPC?
15:21 - 16:00 Marcus Li: yes, Private options include a customer VPC control plane and connectors. KMS integrations are supported; we can do either Redwood-managed keys or customer KMS for encryption at rest. we'll attach our security pack.

16:01 - 17:30 Carla Diaz: and what about data retention and logs as they relate to billing? we don't want PII moving to third-party.
17:31 - 18:20 Sofia Chen: understood — we have options to disable data retention or keep logs in your project. for hosted API we have stricter controls and contractual provisions for data handling; for Private you keep the control plane.

18:25 - 19:40 Tanya Gomez: on latency tradeoffs — how much does batching for throughput trade off against P95 for short requests? our access pattern has many spikes.
19:41 - 20:30 Marcus Li: batching increases throughput efficiency but can add a queuing delay. Redwood runtime supports dynamic batching with latency SLOs; you can pin a percentage of capacity to low-latency lanes and let the rest batch. For spikes we recommend autoscaling with burst capacity.
20:31 - 21:10 Raj Patel: can autoscale handle sudden 10x spikes with bounded cold-start latency?
21:11 - 22:00 Marcus Li: depends on instance types and warm pool. With dedicated you can keep a warm buffer; with hosted we propose a burst SLA and cross-region fallback to avoid long cold starts. We'll show numbers in the perf plan.

22:05 - 23:20 Carla Diaz: procurement question — what commit terms are typical, and do you offer early-termination credits if usage is below commit?
23:21 - 24:05 Sofia Chen: typical commits are 6-12 months; we can structure ramp clauses and make sure the pricing sheet shows step-downs. Early termination is negotiable, often with a graduated credit schedule. we'll put options in the proposal.

24:10 - 26:00 Raj Patel: about quantization — what is Redwood's experience running quantized LLMs for production? accuracy regressions?
26:01 - 27:00 Marcus Li: we run multiple quantization profiles and recommend evaluating quality/regression on your eval prompts. some models tolerate 4-bit quantization with minimal quality loss; others need 8-bit. Redwood Optimize can suggest the quant profile by workload.

27:01 - 28:00 Tanya Gomez: can we do canary rollouts of quantized variants per route? e.g. model v1 on 95% and quantized v1-q on 5%
28:01 - 28:45 Marcus Li: yes, rollouts and automatic fallback are part of the console. you can route by policy and monitor quality metrics.

29:00 - 31:00 Sofia Chen: let's walk through an example runbook: 1) send anonymized traces, 2) Redwood runs bench with hosted and dedicated configs, 3) we produce a token-econ sheet and recommended hosting mix, 4) scope pilot. Agreed?
31:01 - 31:30 Carla Diaz: yes that sounds good.
31:31 - 32:50 Raj Patel: one more — compliance: do you support SAML/SSO and RBAC for team controls?
32:51 - 33:25 Marcus Li: yes SSO and full RBAC. For Private deployments we can integrate with your IdP.

33:26 - 34:10 Carla Diaz: timeline check — can you get the pricing sheet and security docs in a few days? we want to present to procurement next week.
34:11 - 35:00 Sofia Chen: yes; Sofia will send the packet by end of week. Marcus will follow with the bench plan.

35:05 - 36:30 Tanya Gomez: about cost mitigation — do you have multi-model routing, like cheaper smaller models for simple tasks and large models for complex requests?
36:31 - 37:15 Marcus Li: absolutely. smart routing by request type and cost tier is a primary lever. You can route to a smaller quantized model for NLU classification and escalate to a bigger model for generation. Caching can also reduce calls.
37:16 - 38:00 Raj Patel: can Redwood show an example routing policy we can test?
38:01 - 38:45 Marcus Li: yes, we'll include a sample policy and the console screenshots.

38:50 - 41:00 Carla Diaz: back to budgeting — what are typical unit economics for highly repetitive support prompts when caching is in play? ballpark numbers?
41:01 - 42:10 Marcus Li: for high-repeat templates, effective per-use token cost can drop significantly — sometimes down to 20-40% of raw per-token cost once you account for prefix cache hits and cached responses. but need your trace to be precise.
42:11 - 43:00 Sofia Chen: that's why the bench is key — it quantifies wins and exposes edge cases.

43:05 - 44:00 Raj Patel: one operational ask — what monitoring hooks do you expose (trace ids, distributed tracing integrations)?
44:01 - 44:40 Marcus Li: we support tracing hooks and per-token cost breakdowns per request, plus exported logs to your SIEM.

44:45 - 46:00 Carla Diaz: ok last procurement point — invoicing cadence and currency support? we need monthly USD invoicing and PO support.
46:01 - 46:30 Sofia Chen: monthly invoices with PO are standard; we can adapt currency if needed for enterprise.

46:35 - 48:10 Sofia Chen: recap: we'll send pricing, security pack, bench plan. Customer to share anonymized traces and traffic profile. Plan bench week of 7/14. Any blockers?
48:11 - 48:45 Carla Diaz: main blocker is internal signoff timeline, but if we have numbers quickly that's fine.
48:46 - 50:05 Raj Patel: timeline ok. Marcus, please include cold-start numbers for burst scenarios.
50:06 - 50:40 Marcus Li: will do, include p50/p95/p99 and cold-start distributions.
50:41 - 51:30 Sofia Chen: great — thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the packet.
51:31 - 52:00 Carla Diaz: thanks, bye.

Notes: transcription contains small errors (speaker overlap, model names may be mis-typed). References made to shared artifacts: "pricing spreadsheet" (to be shared), "security pack (SOC2 + network diagrams)", "benchmark plan".
notes: P95 latency target for short prompts: <400ms
